items.story_key: story|title:open source version of cyclon phone where ai is the interface
items.content_excerpt: OpenCyclone is a free, open-source version that converts your Android phone into an AI phone. Someone else designed your phone. You already paid for it. We wrote an app. Together they do the thing: you ask, and your phone gets it done. It works in your apps on a hidden screen while you keep using your phone. Before anything is sent, paid, or deleted, it stops and shows you exactly what will happen. Ask for the tool you need. The phone writes a small app, tests it, fixes it, and puts it on your home page. Change it by asking again. Bring your own model: sign in with ChatGPT, use OpenRouter, paste a key, or point it at a model on your own network. Add tools through the Model Context Protocol. Keep the apps you already use. The agent works inside them with your accounts, follows the rules you set, and never opens the apps on your protected list. The approval gate is code, not a promise in a prompt. You can read it, test it, and change it. That is what the word "open" is for. We will run OpenCyclone on two public benchmarks for phone agents and publish every result here, including the failures. Each task is scored by checking the app itself, not by asking the agent if it succeeded. 116 tasks in 20 real apps, from Google Research. Most phone agents report this score, so ours can stand next to theirs. 201 harder tasks, published at ACL 2026. It also tests whether the agent asks you when a request leaves out a fact, and whether it can use connected tools. Neither benchmark checks that an agent stops before it sends or pays. We will publish that test too: the agent must reach the Send button and wait for you, every time. An open-source AI agent for stock Android. It reads the screen of your apps on a hidden display, decides what to tap, and asks you before any action that cannot be taken back. $0. There is no deposit, no pre-order, and no delivery date. You install it today on the phone you have. You pay only your model provider, and a local model costs nothing. Because it is easy to build. An AI phone is an app, a helper process, and a model. One person built this one with AI coding agents, on top of an existing open-source project. Nobody should buy a new phone to get it. An Android phone with Android 12 or later, a computer for a one-time setup script, and an account with a model provider. It was built and tested on a Pixel 7. No. It is early software, written fast. items.content_excerpt: Portal2Bench measures whether AI agents can solve Portal 2's test chambers. Each chamber is a fresh, independent run, scored solved only if the agent finishes within $30 and 300 plans. † Most chambers are still being run, due to compute constraints and usage limits. Yes. GPT-6.1 Sol (Codex) solves 20 of 26 Portal 2 test chambers. GPT-6 Astra (Codex) solves 20, GPT-6.1 Terra (Codex) 19, Opus 5.5 (Claude Code) 11, Sonnet 5.5 (Claude Code) 6, GPT-6 Luna (Codex) 0 and Fable 5.1 (Claude Code) 3 of 15 so far. Portal2Bench pauses Portal 2 while the model thinks. The agent sends keys and view turns, and gets back screenshots and its position. It has a notes folder, but no shell, web or console. Each chamber is a fresh run, solved if the agent reaches the next map within 300 plans and $30. 26 chambers from chapters 2 to 5 count. Each model runs in its own harness at its highest effort. Portal2Bench prices each run at API list prices. A solved chamber's median cost runs from $0.74 (GPT-6.1 Terra) to $13.12 (Fable 5.1). No. The agent has no shell or web, and its file tools reach only its own notes folder. A QA check flags anything else. items.title: Adapting to AI penetration testing orchestrators: The Modern Security Model
items.story_key: story|title:adapting to ai penetration testing orchestrators the modern security model
items.content_excerpt: Over the last month, the number of Large Language Model (LLM) penetration testing and orchestration frameworks has exploded. Just a few weeks ago, ARTEX — an open source agentic penetration testing system that automates offensive security workflows — was the only framework available. In just the last three days, we have seen over 50 framework families attempt to scan Cloudflare customers globally. The number of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses seen running these frameworks has grown into the thousands and continues to increase daily. The proliferation of these frameworks has significantly changed the status quo in cyber defense: defenders are struggling to keep up with the volumetric nature of these autonomously guided attacks. ARTEX was taken down by its creator Autumn-27 on October 8. (“The malicious exploitation of this tool runs entirely counter to its original intent,” they wrote in Chinese. ) But in the month since, the ecosystem has exploded with new fragmented versions of it. There are now over 12,000 repositories, with several hundred unique forks containing lineage from the original repository. Additionally, hundreds of other similar agentic orchestration frameworks have been created since October 8. Daily requests of AI penetration testing (pentesting) and exploitation tools has grown by 30x since October 1. These tools have also begun chaining stolen customer credentials in some of the more complex attacks, such as lateral movement chaining throughout an environment. We expect these frameworks to continue to proliferate, and every organization should be prepared to address this threat. To counter LLM-based pentest frameworks, we recommend that all organizations adopt what we call the Modern Security Model, which has six key pillars: Open-source pentesting frameworks are able to orchestrate AI agents to carry out stages of the traditional Cyber Kill Chain at scale. Tools like ARTEX have the ability to quickly plug in existing Model Context Protocol (MCP) and connect traditional standalone pentesting tools in novel ways. Some even allow operator direction on what type of task to accomplish. These tools can map and enumerate environments, both from the inside and outside. ARTEX and its forks map assets and environments onto a graph, allowing multiple independent parallel agents to enumerate, verify, prototype, and attack at the speed of inference. Release: llm-gemini 0.37

Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.

It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:

Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output
Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Hydrogen   $1.50 $0.075 $7.50

Carbon and Argon are the same price, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.

Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.

I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans. Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:

Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.

Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models:

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.

items.title: Can KV Cache Be Reused Across Model Updates? A DeepSeek-V4-Flash Case Study
items.summary: Reusing key--value (KV) caches across language model updates could avoid repeated computation of shared context, but changes in model weights raise a fundamental question about what these caches preserve. We investigate direct cache reuse across four model updates, with a detailed study of DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Flash-0731. Our central finding is that caches can retain useful task information without faithfully reproducing the updated model's behavior. Retrieval accuracy varies substantially across updates, ranging from near-native performance to large losses. With source caches already available, reuse achieves median time-to-first-token speedups of $2.10$--$5.08\times$ on three longer-prefix QA benchmarks. To characterize the behavioral differences behind these outcomes, we introduce Functional Cache Divergence, which compares next-token distributions under reused and native caches. Direct KV cache reuse better preserves native model behavior in natural-text continuation, whereas compatibility degrades with increasing prefix length in single-token retrieval tasks. Answer-margin analyses help explain how correct retrieval decisions survive substantial internal state changes. Yet even agreement on the first generated token does not ensure agreement in answer content or stopping behavior. These findings establish task utility and fidelity to native inference as distinct criteria for evaluating cross-version KV cache reuse.

items.title: Shortcuts or Memorisation? Revisiting Data Corruption in Natural Language Understanding with Large Language Models
items.summary: Pre-trained encoders fine-tuned on natural language inference (NLI) and other language understanding tasks keep much of their accuracy after the input is perturbed, e.g. by removing all nouns or shuffling the words. Does the same hold for large language models (LLMs), and if so, is it because they have seen the benchmarks during pre-training? In this paper we revisit these perturbation experiments with eight LLMs alongside fine-tuned encoders on GLUE and the three rounds of ANLI. Regardless of model size, every system that answers directly retains 36-72% of its above-chance performance without nouns on MNLI compared to only 14-29% on ANLI. Only a model that reasons before answering departs from this pattern. We also check contamination indicators (including exact $n$-gram counts in the public pre-training data of two of the models) and find no link between exposure and robustness. Our strongest evidence comes from 368 new, human-validated items that none of the models can have seen. All eight LLMs keep more of their performance without nouns on items written in MNLI's style than on items written without its cues. When the perturbation instead removes the function words carrying such cues, this advantage reverses. In light of these results, we argue that robustness to perturbation on familiar NLI benchmarks reflects dataset shortcuts rather than memorisation, and tells us more about the benchmark than about the model.

items.title: SAGE-QA: Semantic-Aware, Grounded Evaluation for Closed-Context Question Answering on SQuAD 2.0
items.summary: Closed-context question answering (QA) requires a system to generate an answer strictly supported by a supplied passage, or to abstain when the passage lacks adequate evidence. SQuAD 2.0 is a widely used benchmark for this setting, scored by Exact Match (EM) i.e., character-level agreement with human reference spans after lexical normalization. For generative large language models (LLMs), however, an EM failure may reflect a valid paraphrase or an alternative passage-supported answer rather than a hallucination. The best prior leaderboard EM is approximately 91%, but evaluating generative models requires separating lexical divergence from factual error. We introduce SAGE-QA (Semantic-Aware, Grounded Evaluation for Question Answering), a multi-tiered framework combining reference-based Semantic Equivalence Scoring (SES) and passage-based Re-Validation Scoring (RVS). On a fixed set of 10,000 SQuAD 2.0 validation examples, we compute EM and decision-matrix F1 from TP, TN, FP, and FN counts for zero-shot closed-weight frontier models and for open-weight models, untuned and fine-tuned. Zero-shot, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro reach 85.21 and 86.66 EM, outperforming untuned Llama 3 8B (56.88), gpt-oss-20b (66.28), and Llama 3.3 70B (71.39). Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adds 21.19 to 34.06 EM points, raising these models to 90.94, 87.47, and 94.24 EM, respectively. Auditing the frontier models with SAGE-QA and an external LLM judge yields dataset-wide SES scores of 92.81 for Claude Opus 4.6 and 91.67 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and hybrid RVS scores, which combine benchmark credit with passage-based judge assessments, of 97.96 and 98.02. Fine-tuned open-weight models perform best, with fine-tuned Llama 3.3 70B surpassing the previous best known EM.

On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows. I'm hoping they fix that in the future - it would be great if you could download a single binary and use that as part of a standard test suite in other languages and on other platforms.

items.content_excerpt: The current Claude lineup has four generally available models: Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs. If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code , you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs. The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium . There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work. Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate. Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model. Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page . When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. When you pick a larger model, for example, you are choosing capability over latency. These are the main trade-offs to think through. Generally, bigger models cost more per token and are more capable, but the cost vs capability trade-off isn't universally true at the task level. A higher price per token doesn't always mean a higher cost per task, or a better result. items.title: Inkling 2 Small on vLLM: Day-0 Support
items.summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|variant:small|title:inkling 2 small on vllm day 0 support
items.content_excerpt: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small on day 0. It is a multimodal (text and vision) MoE model with 594B total and 17B active parameters and up to 1M tokens of context. The model also comes with a native DSpark speculator. vLLM supports it with optimized performance (up to 630 TPS/user at TP4 and acceptance length 3.5) and also supports LoRA. Figure 1. Inkling 2 Small architecture. Gold marks what is new or changed since Inkling. Inkling backbone + recent advances. Inkling 2 Small keeps Inkling's backbone: the 5:1 mix of sliding-window and full attention, GQA with a learned relative bias instead of RoPE, the four short convolutions per layer and a sigmoid-routed MoE. On top of it, it adds recent advances. Block attention residuals replace the residual stream, so before each sublayer a learned query mixes the outputs of earlier 6-layer blocks. Gated attention puts a sigmoid gate on each head's output, together with a per-token attention sink . It replaces the hMLP image encoder with a 23-layer ViT. Mixed-precision MoE with Four-Over-Six NVFP4. Out of Inkling 2 Small's 48 layers, the experts of the first 40 use NVFP4 and those of the last 8 use MXFP8. The NVFP4 activations use a per-token global scale plus dual-candidate block scales ( Four Over Six ): for each 16-element block, the quantizer tries scaling the block's maximum to 6 and to 4, and keeps whichever gives the lower reconstruction error (MAE). DSpark speculator with an RNN head. The checkpoint also ships a DSpark draft in place of Inkling's 8 chained MTP heads. The speculator has 5 layers and drafts 7 tokens per step. The head is the RNN variant that DeepSeek's DSpark paper described. Kernel fusion and PDL. vLLM aggressively fuses the collective communication and memory-bound ops between sublayers into a single kernel. With attention residuals, each boundary needs an all-reduce, a short convolution, a residual update, the attention-residual mix and an RMSNorm: five memory-bound steps on the same hidden states. The fused kernel, allreduce_conv_mix (gold in Figure 2), runs the all-reduce over NVLink multicast and keeps everything after it in registers. The GEMM, attention, routing and activation kernels launch with programmatic dependent launch (PDL), so each one's prologue overlaps the tail of the previous kernel, which matters at small batch sizes, where a decode step is a long chain of short kernels. items.title: Introducing new AI functions for AlloyDB: ai.classify and ai.extract
items.summary:
Transactional databases store vast amounts of unstructured text — clinical notes, customer reviews, support tickets, invoices, and property descriptions. Historically, working with this text meant building complex application code: You had to export data from the database, call external model endpoints, write custom prompt wrappers, parse unpredictable responses, manage retry logic, and update database records. This application-side loop creates operational friction. It introduces query latency, bloats application code, increases model token costs, and creates data compliance risks by moving sensitive information across multiple network boundaries.

We built AlloyDB AI to bring Gemini world knowledge directly into your operational database. Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a disconnected external service, we integrated model intelligence directly into the database engine. Today, we are announcing the preview of two new SQL functions in the AlloyDB AI query engine — ai.classify and ai.extract — available in the google_ml_integration extension (version 1.6.1 or later) on PostgreSQL 18, allowing you to perform classification and structured extraction directly inside your database using standard SQL. Supported by smart batching for AI functions (previously known as AI Function Acceleration), these functions deliver production scalability and performance. 

Now, let’s take a look at these new functions and how to use them.

Classifying text directly in SQL with ai.classify

The ai.classify function categorizes text into user-defined classes without requiring manual prompt engineering. You can specify categories as a simple list of labels or provide a list containing label names and descriptions to guide model context.

Key capabilities include:

  • Single-label classification (output_mode => 'single') to assign the single best category

  • Multi-label classification (output_mode => 'multi') to return all matching categories

  • Category descriptions using 2D arrays to provide explicit context for each label

  • Few-shot prompting by supplying inline examples

  • Flexible execution modes for individual rows (TEXT), arrays (TEXT[]), and cursors (REFCURSOR)

Here’s a quick example showing how you can classify customer feedback directly within a SQL query:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SET google_ml_integration.enable_preview_ai_functions = TRUE;\r\n\r\nCREATE TABLE product_reviews (id INT, review TEXT);\r\n\r\nINSERT INTO product_reviews VALUES\r\n(1, 'Fantastic, would buy again!'),\r\n(2, 'Broken on arrival.'),\r\n(3, 'Mediocre, not worth the price.');\r\n\r\nSELECT unnest(\r\n ai.classify(\r\n inputs => ARRAY(SELECT review FROM product_reviews ORDER BY id),\r\n categories => ARRAY[\r\n ['positive', 'Good sentiment'],\r\n ['neutral', 'Neither good nor bad sentiment'],\r\n ['negative', 'Bad sentiment']\r\n ],\r\n batch_size => 5\r\n )\r\n) AS sentiment;\r\n\r\n-- Expected Output:\r\n-- sentiment\r\n-- ---------\r\n-- positive\r\n-- negative\r\n-- negative"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fc6de247610>)])]>

Extracting structured JSON with ai.extract

The ai.extract function transforms unstructured text into structured JSON data matching your target schema — specified as a JSON schema or a text list of fields. It handles system instructions internally, saving you from writing prompt templates or response parsers.

Key capabilities include:

  • Schema flexibility supporting standard JSON schemas or plain text field lists

  • Automatic transformation of unstructured text into machine-readable JSON

  • Overloaded function signatures for single rows, arrays, and cursor batching

Here’s an example extracting clinical fields from free-form medical notes:

code_block

She is currently experiencing a mild fever, persistent cough, and severe body aches. Speeding up queries with smart batching

Running AI evaluations row-by-row can slow down query execution. AlloyDB addresses this with smart batching for AI functions. When you use ai.classify or ai.extract in SQL WHERE clause expressions, the database engine automatically groups inputs into optimized micro-batches before sending them to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform models.

Smart batching delivers significant performance and efficiency improvements:

  • Faster inference for query execution compared to row-at-a-time evaluations

  • Reduces total model token spend by optimizing input prompt overhead

Real-world industry applications

Native classification and extraction functions support operational workflows across key industry sectors:

  • Healthcare: Securely convert free-text clinical notes into structured records containing patient names, symptoms, and prescribed medications, keeping patient data safely within the confines of the database.

  • Financial services: Extract vendor details, invoice dates, and line-item totals from scanned document text.

  • Legal technology: Pull governing law, liability caps, and termination notice periods from contract documents.

  • Real estate: Extract property types, bedroom counts, and price ranges from descriptive listing text.

  • Knowledge graphs: Extract entities and relationships from documents to populate PostgreSQL Property Graph (PGQ) structures.

Next steps and getting started

We are continuing to expand in-database AI capabilities in AlloyDB, with upcoming enhancements planned for advanced cost optimization, line-level provenance tracking, and query pushdowns beyond WHERE clauses.

To start using ai.classify and ai.extract in your database:

  • Review the AlloyDB AI Query Engine documentation.

  • Explore the AlloyDB release notes.
